document_title: Texas A&M plans an AI foundry for new alloys
_note: Slide strings read off the render report's text nodes and each frame's own source line by build_copy.py.
caption:
Why does an AI lab melt metal?

Several dozen elements make roughly a trillion possible mixes. That sounds like a job for software. Raymundo Arróyave of Texas A&M says no computational tool anywhere can predict how an alloy will behave.

A $2 million WoodNext Foundation grant will help build the Aggie AI Foundry. Computer controlled arms on an assembly line are to mix, melt and test new alloys. The university says existing self driving labs can't handle alloys at up to 3,000 degrees Celsius. Months of work cut to a week or less is the goal, not a result.

A separate NSF award has obligated $4.1 million of an estimated $24.9 million. It funds the open access Autonomous Robotic Metallurgist at Texas A&M.

The award record names researchers at non-R1 and EPSCoR institutions among its intended users. Who outside Texas A&M makes the first alloy there?

S2.headline: Roughly a trillion ways to mix them

S3.headline: $2 million, in buttons
S3.body: The WoodNext Foundation manages the philanthropy of Roku's founder, Anthony Wood, and his wife Susan. The grant comes through a donor advised fund. Each button is an equal share of the grant, 20 in all. Drawn to illustrate.

S4.headline: Mix, melt and test, on one line
S4.body: Robotics will mix, melt and test the materials with computer controlled arms along an assembly line that takes samples, the university says. It says existing self driving labs can't handle alloys at up to 3,000 degrees Celsius. Drawn to illustrate.

S5.headline: Two researchers, more than 100 papers
S5.body: Ibrahim Karaman, who heads the department, and Raymundo Arróyave conceived the foundry. They have published more than 100 papers together. The university calls it the first lab of its kind in academia. Drawn to illustrate.

S6.headline: NSF has obligated $4.1 million of $24.9 million
S6.body: The $24.9 million is the award's estimated total. Its Autonomous Robotic Metallurgist at Texas A&M is built to design, make, test and learn from new alloys. In front, the WoodNext grant at $100,000 a button. Drawn to illustrate.

S7.headline: Six years, one bar a month
S7.body: The NSF award runs from September 1st to August 31st, 2032. The platform is open access, and its intended users include researchers at non-R1 and EPSCoR institutions. One bar is one month. Drawn to illustrate.

S8.headline: No computational tool can predict it, Arróyave says
S8.body: Arróyave says no computational tool anywhere in the world can predict how an alloy is going to behave. His NSF backed PhaseForge applies machine learning to CALPHAD to say whether a material can exist at all. Drawn to illustrate.

S9.headline: So the metal still gets tested
S9.body: Texas A&M's goal is alloys in a week or less instead of months, a target and not a result. PhaseForge is free online and anyone can contribute to it. The NSF platform is open access. Drawn to illustrate.
